The last commit I made was marking task #1 as completed. After that I added the new modules and tests, but I haven't yet committed those new files. To keep the project's history clean and to ensure the CI pipeline (or any future runs) sees these changes, I should stage all the new/modified files and make a commit.

Which files have changed? Let's recap:
- src/mythosmini/leaderboard/scoring.py (new)
- src/mythosmini/leaderboard/placement.py (new)
- src/mythosmini/leaderboard/fetch.py (new)
- tests/fixtures/leaderboard_index.html (added via cp)

The safest approach is to add everything under src/mythosmini, the test file, the fixtures directory, and the requirements.txt. Using `git add -A` with those paths will stage all modifications, additions, and deletions. Then I can commit with a concise message describing the addition of config and leaderboard modules along with their proving tests. I don't need to open an editor; I can use `-qm` to set the commit message directly.

After committing, I want to verify that the commit succeeded and see the latest commit hash/message. Running `git log --oneline -1` will output the most recent commit line, confirming the operation.

Thus, the next logical action is to execute a Bash command that adds the relevant paths, commits with the appropriate message, and shows the latest log entry. This aligns with the workflow of finalizing changes after successful tests and linting. I'll construct the command accordingly.

Command:
`git add -A src/mythosmini tests/test_leaderboard.py tests/fixtures requirements.txt && git commit -qm "add config and leaderboard modules with proving tests" && git log --oneline -1`

This will stage all new/modified files, commit them with the message, and print the short log line. That's exactly what I need to do now.
